claims.text: Catalytic activity of nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts in ethanol oxidation is governed by electronic-structure modulation caused by atomic-scale lattice distortions.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions enhance oxygen adsorption and activation at the catalyst surface.
The initial catalyst is a nanoscale, compositionally and structurally uniform PtPdRhRuIrOs solid solution.
Varying the atomic ratios of Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, Ir, and Os can systematically change lattice distortion or strain.
The proposed operating conditions are 60–80 °C, ambient pressure, and an acidic electrolyte such as 0.1 M HClO4.
Lattice distortions alter the d-band center of the catalyst surface.
Changes in the surface d-band center modulate the adsorption energy of oxygen species.
Modulation of oxygen-species adsorption enhances ethanol-oxidation activity.
Catalysts with moderate lattice distortions will have higher current density than catalysts with minimal lattice distortions.
Catalysts with moderate lattice distortions will have higher current density than catalysts with excessive lattice distortions.
The activity maximum at moderate distortion arises from optimized oxygen adsorption and activation.
An equiatomic catalyst with no intentionally imposed lattice strain is the baseline.
The hypothesized relationship applies to solid-solution particles smaller than 10 nm under acidic conditions.
Within the stated boundary, lattice distortions significantly influence electronic structure.
The exact relationship between lattice-distortion magnitude and catalytic activity is not well defined.
The hypothesis assumes that electronic effects dominate over surface segregation and particle-size effects.
